# Understanding tensor contractions through reshaping

Consider a rank-3 tensor

$$
T_{ijk},
$$

with dimensions

$$
\dim(i)=2,\qquad \dim(j)=2,\qquad \dim(k)=3,
$$

and a rank-2 tensor

$$
M_{lm},
$$

with

$$
\dim(l)=\dim(m)=2.
$$

Thus,

$$
T\in\mathbb{C}^{2\times2\times3},
\qquad
M\in\mathbb{C}^{2\times2}.
$$

One possible way of visualizing $T$ is as three $2\times2$ slices, one for each value of $k$:

$$
T[:,:,1]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
T_{111} & T_{121}\\
T_{211} & T_{221}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
T[:,:,2]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
T_{112} & T_{122}\\
T_{212} & T_{222}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
T[:,:,3]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
T_{113} & T_{123}\\
T_{213} & T_{223}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
M_{11} & M_{12}\\
M_{21} & M_{22}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

## Before contracting: the dimensions must match

Suppose we first tried to contract the third index of $T$ with either
index of $M$.

This is impossible, because

$$
\dim(k)=3,
$$

whereas both indices of $M$ have dimension 2.

A contraction requires the two indices being paired to have the same
dimension. This is analogous to the requirement that the inner
dimensions agree in ordinary matrix multiplication.

Instead, let us contract the first two indices of $T$ with the two
indices of $M$, in order:

$$
i\leftrightarrow l,
\qquad
j\leftrightarrow m.
$$

In the Julia interface, this contraction is written as

```julia
contract(T, M, [1 => 1, 2 => 2])
```

Mathematically, it corresponds to

$$
C_k
=
\sum_{i,j} T_{ijk}M_{ij}.
$$

Only $k$ remains uncontracted, so the result is a rank-1 tensor.

The original tensors have ranks 3 and 2. Since each contraction removes
one index from each tensor, contracting two pairs gives

$$
\operatorname{rank}(C)
=
3+2-2(2)
=
1.
$$

## Turning the contraction into matrix multiplication

The useful computational idea is to combine several tensor indices into
a single **fused index**.

For $T_{ijk}$, the contracted indices are $i$ and $j$. We combine them
into a single index

$$
I=(i,j).
$$

The remaining index $k$ stays explicit:

$$
T_{ijk}
\longrightarrow
\widetilde{T}_{kI}.
$$

Since

$$
\dim(k)=3
$$

and

$$
\dim(I)=\dim(i)\dim(j)=2\times2=4,
$$

the rank-3 tensor can be represented as a $3\times4$ matrix.

For $M_{lm}$, both indices are contracted, so they can also be fused
into a single index,

$$
I=(l,m),
$$

giving a vector of dimension

$$
2\times2=4.
$$

Thus, the original tensor contraction has become an ordinary
matrix-vector multiplication:

$$
C_k
=
\sum_I \widetilde{T}_{kI}\widetilde{M}_I.
$$

## The ordering of a fused index matters

There is one subtle point that is easy to overlook.

Writing

$$
I=(i,j)
$$

does not, by itself, specify which integer value of $I$ corresponds to
each pair $(i,j)$.

For example, we could enumerate the pairs as

$$
(1,1),\ (2,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,2),
$$

or instead as

$$
(1,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,1),\ (2,2).
$$

Either convention is mathematically valid.

What matters is that **the same convention must be used for both
tensors**. Otherwise, matrix multiplication would pair tensor entries
corresponding to different values of the original indices.

For Julia arrays, it is natural to use Julia's column-major ordering.
For a $2\times2$ array, the entries are traversed as

$$
(1,1),\ (2,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,2).
$$

Before reshaping $T$, we first permute its indices so that the
uncontracted index $k$ appears first and the contracted indices $i,j$
appear together:

$$
T_{ijk}
\longrightarrow
T_{kij}.
$$

We then fuse the contracted pair $(i,j)$ into a single index,

$$
T_{kij}
\longrightarrow
\widetilde T_{k(ij)}.
$$

In the following equations, fused indices are enclosed in parentheses
to emphasize that several original tensor indices are being represented
by a single composite index. The parentheses have no additional
mathematical meaning.

Using Julia's column-major convention, we obtain

$$
\widetilde{M}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
M_{(11)}\\
M_{(21)}\\
M_{(12)}\\
M_{(22)}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

while the permuted and reshaped tensor $T$ becomes

$$
\widetilde{T}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
T_{1(11)} & T_{1(21)} & T_{1(12)} & T_{1(22)}\\
T_{2(11)} & T_{2(21)} & T_{2(12)} & T_{2(22)}\\
T_{3(11)} & T_{3(21)} & T_{3(12)} & T_{3(22)}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Here, the first index labels the surviving $k$ index, while the
parenthesized pair represents the fused $(i,j)$ index.

Their product is

$$
\widetilde{T}\widetilde{M}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_{i,j}T_{ij1}M_{ij}\\
\sum_{i,j}T_{ij2}M_{ij}\\
\sum_{i,j}T_{ij3}M_{ij}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

which is precisely the desired contraction

$$
C_k
=
\sum_{i,j}T_{ijk}M_{ij}.
$$

The important point is therefore not that there is a unique way to fuse
tensor indices. Rather, the ordering chosen for the fused contracted
index must be **consistent on both sides of the contraction**.

This is what allows a general tensor contraction to be reduced to
ordinary matrix multiplication:

$$
\boxed{
\text{permute indices}
\longrightarrow
\text{fuse indices with reshape}
\longrightarrow
\text{matrix multiplication}
\longrightarrow
\text{reshape the result}
}
$$

The permutation step becomes necessary when the contracted and
uncontracted indices are not already arranged in the appropriate order.
